study.title: Psalm 137 - I'm sorry in exile and cry for righteousness
study.overview: Psalm 137 expresses Israel's pain in Babylonian captivity. First, the people weep on the banks of the rivers of Babylon and refuse to turn into entertainment the songs connected with Zion. Then the psalmist affirms his allegiance to Jerusalem, saying that he cannot treat the holy city as something forgettable. Finally, the poem passes from the wounded memory to a hard cry for justice against Edom and Babylon, ending with a bliss linked to retribution against the oppressors. The psalm does not describe cold feelings; it reveals a traumatized faith that leads to pain before God.

outline.title: I'm sorry in exile and refusal to sing
outline.explanation: The initial verses show captive Jews crying on foreign land. The harps are hung because Zion's songs do not match the humiliation of exile, nor with the insolent request of the oppressors for the losers to sing as if nothing had happened.

outline.title: Memory of Jerusalem as a commitment to loyalty
outline.explanation: Here the psalmist makes a solemn vow: not to forget Jerusalem, nor to allow the city to get out of the centre of its joys. The remembrance of Zion is treated as part of the very spiritual identity of the people of God.

outline.title: Clamor for justice against enemies
outline.explanation: The psalm recalls the violence and betrayal of Edom, who would have rejoiced and collaborated in the ruin of Jerusalem. Then Babylon is presented as guilty and destined for judgment; the final language is a severe imprecity, an expression of desire for divine retribution, not a simple invitation to personal revenge.

study.context: The notes indicate that the psalm was composed in the period of captivity in Babylon, when the people of God were humbled among the conquerors. The commentators observe the link between the memory of Zion and the pain of exile. They also highlight Edom's hostility on the day of the fall of Jerusalem, mentioning their participation or support for the destruction of the city. It is not safe to say more than that only on the basis of the notes provided.
study.theology: The Psalm teaches that true worship cannot be reduced to spectacle, especially when the people of God are under discipline and pain. The longing of Jerusalem shows that the covenant with the Lord includes memory, identity and fidelity to its place of dwelling among the people. At the same time, the text shows that the Bible does not hide the tension between suffering and justice: prayer can include deep mourning and even severe requests for retribution. Theologically, this presents God as the one who sees oppression, records betrayal and will judge the enemies of his people. Still, the psalm should be read as a poetic and historical prayer of a wounded people, not as a simple norm to act cruelly.

scholarViews.insight: The psalmist responds to the pain of exile with a resolution of remembering Jerusalem, and includes a surprising prayer of revenge against enemies.
The captives cannot rejoice or satisfy the oppressors, because they are under humiliation and mourning; the scene expresses deep sorrow of the people of God.
The harps hanging in the willows form a moving frame of withdrawal from singing, as the affliction made the joyful music unfit on foreign land.

questions: What place does the remembrance of God and his city occupy when faith goes through humiliation and loss?
How does the psalm help us to distinguish between lament before God and personal vengeance?
How do we react when we are tempted to treat sacred things as if they were only religious entertainment?
study.practice: Bring to God your losses without disguising them. If you are in the phase of shame, inner exile or spiritual frustration, do as the psalmist: name the pain, preserve the memory of what is holy and refuse to trivialize worship. Also examine whether there is a tendency in you to want faith to serve the taste of others rather than to remain faithful to the Lord. Finally, giving God the desire for righteousness, rather than trying to execute it with their own hands.
study.uncertainty: Notes do not allow the authorship or the exact date of the psalm. The language of verse 9 is a poetic imprecation and should not be read as direct authorization for violence. It is also not possible to accurately define, only with this data, all the historical details of the involvement of Edom and Babylon beyond what the commentators record.
